youtube_video.title: DIFOT Formula and Worked Example for Australian and NZ Manufacturers
youtube_video.description:
Read the full guide: https://zudoworks.com/insights/difot-delivery-in-full-on-time/

DIFOT means delivery in full, on time. It is the delivery score Australian and New Zealand customers ask their suppliers for, and buyers elsewhere usually call it OTIF. The formula is one line. The hard part is deciding what counts as in full and what counts as on time, because two shops with the same deliveries can report very different figures. This 50-second explainer walks through the formula, a worked example, the multiplication trap, and the five rules to agree before the number means anything.

Chapters
00:00 What DIFOT means
00:03 One order line, two tests
00:10 The DIFOT formula
00:15 Worked example: 129 of 150 lines, 86%
00:22 The trap: never multiply on-time by in-full
00:28 Count by whole order and it drops to 75%
00:33 Five rules to agree first
00:38 A cause for every failed line
00:42 Read the full guide

Key facts from the guide
- A delivery passes only if the full quantity arrives on or before the agreed date. Late, short or both is a failure.
- DIFOT % = deliveries in full and on time ÷ deliveries due × 100. Count everything that was due, including lines not yet delivered.
- Do not multiply an on-time rate by an in-full rate: lines that fail both tests get counted twice.
- Example (invented figures): 150 order lines due, 129 passed, so DIFOT by line is 86.0%. On time alone is 91.3%, in full alone 92.0%. By whole order the same month scores 75.0%, and against the date the customer first asked for it scores 78.0%.
- Agree five rules first: the unit, the date, ship or receipt, the limits, and how split deliveries count.
- There is no universal benchmark. The target that matters is the one in your customer's supply agreement.

The guide also covers DIFOT against OTIF, OTD and DIFOTAI, how to start measuring with a spreadsheet, the common causes of failed deliveries and what to fix first.

Before you send a DIFOT figure to a customer, check how it was calculated.

DIFOT, delivery in full, on time, asks one question of every order line due: did the full quantity arrive by the agreed date? Late, short or both is a failure. The formula is simple. The definitions are where scores drift.

Our worked example (figures invented to show the arithmetic) takes one month at a small fabrication shop: 150 order lines due, 129 passed.

01 By order line: 86.0%
02 By whole order: 75.0%, because one short line fails the whole order
03 On time alone: 91.3%, which looks healthier than it is
04 Against the date the customer first asked for: 78.0%

And one figure that is simply wrong: multiplying the on-time rate by the in-full rate gives 84.0%, because lines that were late and short get counted twice.

None of the other figures is wrong. They answer different questions. That is why the unit, the date, ship or receipt, the tolerances and split deliveries should be agreed and written at the top of the report before anyone quotes a number.

The full guide covers DIFOT against OTIF, how to start measuring with a spreadsheet, and the causes to fix first. Link in the first comment.

linkedin_profile_carousel:
A supplier scorecard arrives with a DIFOT column, and the number in it is lower than the one your team reports internally.

I see this more often than you might expect, and usually nobody has made a mistake. The two sides have simply counted differently.

DIFOT means delivery in full, on time. A line passes only if the full quantity arrives by the agreed date. Easy to say. Then come the decisions:

→ Do you count order lines or whole orders? One short line fails a whole order.

→ Which date? The one you first promised, the one the customer asked for, or the one you quietly moved last week? A date you moved yourself shouldn't count.

→ Ship date or receipt? If you book the freight, the customer feels the receipt date.

→ How much tolerance on quantity and date? And do early deliveries pass?

→ If you split a line, does it pass when the last part lands?

In the worked example in our guide (invented figures), one month of deliveries scores 86% by line, 75% by order and 78% against the customer's requested date. Same trucks, same parts.

There's also one shortcut to avoid: multiplying your on-time rate by your in-full rate. Lines that were late and short get counted twice.

My suggestion is boring but it works. Write the five rules at the top of the report, agree them with whoever deals with your biggest customer, and don't change them month to month. Then put the average promised lead time beside the score, so nobody can buy a better number by quoting longer dates.
